title: How long, Catiline?
saying: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
author: Cicero

Albert Curtis Clark (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1908; Oxford Classical Texts), public domain; as encoded by the Perseus Digital Library (TEI file phi0474.phi013.perseus-lat2, whose header names "Albert Curtis Clark" as editor and "Clarendon", "1908"; markup CC BY-SA 4.0)
edition.section: In Catilinam 1.1 (complete) and the first sentence of 1.2

source_text: quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra? quam diu etiam furor iste tuus nos eludet? quem ad finem sese effrenata iactabit audacia? nihilne te nocturnum praesidium Palati, nihil urbis vigiliae, nihil timor populi, nihil concursus bonorum omnium, nihil hic munitissimus habendi senatus locus, nihil horum ora voltusque moverunt? patere tua consilia non sentis, constrictam iam horum omnium scientia teneri coniurationem tuam non vides? quid proxima, quid superiore nocte egeris, ubi fueris, quos convocaveris, quid consili ceperis quem nostrum ignorare arbitraris? O tempora, o mores! senatus haec intellegit, consul videt; hic tamen vivit.
excerpt_note: Section 1.1 complete and the opening of 1.2, up to "hic tamen vivit." The Perseus file prints sentence-initial words in lower case (it tags them as regularized), so the speech begins "quo usque"; this text keeps the letters exactly. Clark's apparatus notes are left out (e.g. "nos om. A et Iulius Victor": one manuscript, A, and the rhetorician Julius Victor omit nos).

translation: Just how far, Catiline, will you go in abusing our patience? How much longer will that madness of yours keep making fools of us? What limit is there to the swaggering of your unbridled recklessness? Has nothing moved you: not the night guard on the Palatine, not the patrols in the city, not the people's fear, not the rallying of every loyal citizen, not this heavily defended place where the senate is meeting, not the faces and looks of the men here? Do you not realize that your plans are out in the open? Do you not see that your conspiracy is already caught and held, because everyone here knows about it? What you did last night and the night before, where you were, whom you called together, what plan you settled on: which of us do you suppose does not know? What times! What morals! The senate understands all this, the consul sees it; and yet this man is still alive.
translation_note: Abūtēre is the future of the deponent abūtor, with the alternative ending -ēre for -ēris; it takes an ablative (patientiā). Quō ūsque means "up to what point". In Ō tempora, ō mōrēs! the accusatives are exclamations. The repeated nihil ("not at all") is used as an adverb, with all six subjects sharing the one verb mōvērunt. Bonī, "the good", is Cicero's word for loyal, propertied citizens on his side.

essay.t: Cicero was consul in 63 BC; Britannica says the optimates backed his election because they feared the revolutionary ideas of his rival, Catiline.
Sallust adds that the nobility, who had thought a "new man" would pollute the consulship, dropped their jealousy once news of the conspiracy spread.

Catiline planned armed risings and arson, and Cicero struggled to convince the senate until it passed its "last decree"; Britannica dates this to 22 October, a date modern scholars infer rather than read in a source.

Sallust says Catiline came into the senate to look innocent, and that Cicero, from fear of his presence or from anger, gave a brilliant speech useful to the state, which he afterwards wrote out and published.
In a letter to Atticus of 60 BC, Cicero says he is assembling "consular speeches" on the model of Demosthenes' Philippics, among them the one "when I sent Catiline out of the city".
So we read the version Cicero chose to publish; how closely it matches what he said that day cannot be checked.
In my reading, it casts him as the watchful consul who sees everything: "the consul sees".
In the debate on the arrested conspirators, Caesar, in Sallust's account, warned against deciding in anger.
The senate followed Cato. Lentulus was lowered into the Tullianum, a dark, foul cell about twelve feet underground, and strangled with a noose; four others died the same way.
Catiline fell in battle; Sallust says he was found far from his own men among enemy corpses, still breathing.
Britannica says the executions were carried out "on Cicero's responsibility".
Plutarch reports that Cicero announced them by calling out "They have lived", since Romans avoid ill-omened words for death; vixerunt is the Latin that Plutarch's Greek renders.
When Clodius became tribune in 58 BC and Pompey refused help, Cicero left Rome, and Clodius passed a law of doubtful legality declaring him an exile; Pompey and Milo later helped secure his recall.
The famous cry survives in a speech its author shaped for readers as well as for the senate.

questions.q: According to Sallust, what did Cicero do with this speech after giving it?
options: He wrote it out and published it
He had it read aloud in the Forum
He sent it to Pompey in Asia
He kept it secret until his exile

questions.q: What does Sallust say happened to Lentulus?
options: He was strangled in the Tullianum
He escaped to Gaul with Catiline
He was exiled along with Cicero
He died in battle near Catiline

questions.q: Why did the executions later cause trouble for Cicero?
options: Clodius had a law passed declaring him an exile
Catiline's allies took him to court for murder
Caesar had him expelled from the senate
The people voted to cancel his consulship
